On your turn: Move the boat to a new tile. Collect the tile you land on. Try to leave good opportunities for the next player. There is one important twist: In a 3–5 player game, your final score is your own Fishing Score plus the Fishing Score of the player on your left . The game ends when the boat can no longer move. Components 1 Double-Sided Game Board 1 Boat Token 31 Basic Fish Tiles 18 Special Fish Tiles 6 sets of 3 5 Action Tiles 1 of each type Setup 1. Choose the Board Side Place the Game Board in the center of the table. For a 5-player game : Use the side with the Large Central Island . For other player counts: Use the Small Central Island for a shorter game. Use the Large Central Island for a longer game. 2. Prepare the Tiles Choose Special Fish sets based on the board side: Board Side Special Fish Sets Special Fish Tiles Small Central Island 2 sets 6 Large Central Island 4 sets 12 Add the chosen Special Fish Tiles to: All 31 Basic Fish Tiles All 5 Action Tiles Mix all tiles face-down. Place them randomly on the water spaces of the board. 3. Place the Boat Place the Boat Token on the Central Island. 4. Choose the First Player Choose any starting player. For example: The player who most recently went fishing may go first. Gameplay Players take turns moving the shared Boat Token and collecting tiles. On your turn: Move the Boat. Collect the Tile. Then play passes to the next player. Move the Boat At the start of your turn: Move the Boat from its current space to a tile in an adjacent water space . Normally, the Boat must move to an adjacent tile. Exception: Skipjacks allow a special non-adjacent move. Collect the Tile After moving onto a tile: Remove it from the board. Place it face-up in front of you. Keep your collected tiles visible so everyone can see how many of each type you have. If you collect an Action Tile: Resolve its effect immediately. Returning to the Central Island If there are no possible moves from the Boat's current space: Return the Boat to the Central Island. Move the Boat from the Central Island to an adjacent tile. This is the only way the Boat may return to the Central Island. Central Island The Central Island counts as one single space . community_text:
[Rating: 5/10] I like what they are going for but feel like it needed to be polished a bit more. There was one game where the skipjack meant that I had zero options and just took the next fish. Whoever had the most fish in the double points color won every time. We also had a game with a tie which meant that two different people also had a time which felt bad. For now, I have to pass on this game.

[Rating: 5.5/10] Adorable game. This will work for a lot of people. I don't particularly enjoy the scoring system of the game, which is why I rate it lower, but others will find it interesting. You score for what you collect and what the player to your left collects as well. You want to set them up, but not so well that they win. It is a fine line to balance. It was interesting, but not what I would be asking to play.

[Rating: 7/10] Friendly Fishing is a neat semi-cooperative game with map reduction tile collection similar to Hey That's My Fish (except you can only travel one adjacent space). Game arc definitely feels more satisfying than its predecessor Tonari because you reset the player piece after a dead end in this one.

[Rating: 7/10] I like fishing games. The combined scores is somewhat uncommon. The play is super simple and I expect this to get played in a lot of situations. Looks nice.

[Rating: 7/10] Friendly Fishing is an enjoyable game that has some tricky shared incentives. You want to set up a good move while not letting that good move set up a good move. In a 3 player game, you can ideally calculate a whole round ahead. It is a fairly relaxed game, but one with a little bit of depth worth the 20 minutes it takes

[Rating: 7.5/10] A pleasant abstract with good presentation, clean simple rules, and excellent flow. Approachable theme, and enjoyable to play. Abstracts are not my preferred genre but I like this one.
